If you're 50 or older, you can add an extra 8,000 dollars in catch up contributions, for a total of 32,500. And if you're between 60 and 63, there's a bigger catch up limit of 11,250, letting you put in up to 35,750 total. This money comes out of your paycheck before taxes, so maxing it out lowers your taxable income right now, not just your future nest egg. Check with your HR or plan provider to update your contribution percentage today.

Check your filing status and make sure your withholding matches.

topics.title: 2026 Social Security Tax Cap: $184,500 - What High Earners Should Know
topics.script: If you're a higher earner, this 2026 number matters for your paycheck. The Social Security Administration just raised the taxable maximum, also called the wage base, to 184,500 dollars for 2026. That means Social Security tax, the 6.2 percent you see withheld from your paycheck, only applies up to that amount of income. Once your year to date wages cross 184,500 dollars, that specific withholding stops for the rest of the year. If you switch jobs mid year, double check your total withholding across employers, because each employer restarts the calculation separately, and you could end up overpaying. You'd then claim that excess back as a credit on your tax return.

topics.script: This is one of the most overlooked tax credits, and the IRS just updated it for 2026. The maximum Earned Income Tax Credit for families with three or more qualifying children is now 8,231 dollars. The EITC is a refundable credit, meaning even if you owe zero in taxes, you can still get this money back as a refund. It's designed for low to moderate income working individuals and families, and the exact amount depends on your income, filing status, and number of kids. Millions of eligible people skip claiming it every year simply because they don't know it exists or think they don't qualify. Use the IRS EITC assistant tool on IRS dot gov to check your eligibility before you file.

topics.title: 2026 Capital Gains Tax Brackets: 0%, 15%, 20% - New IRS Thresholds
topics.script: Selling stock or property this year? The IRS just updated the income thresholds for long term capital gains taxes in 2026. If you're single and your taxable income is under 49,450 dollars, you pay zero percent tax on long term gains. Between 49,450 and 545,500, you pay 15 percent. Above that, it's 20 percent. If you're married filing jointly, the zero percent bracket goes up to 98,900 dollars, 15 percent applies up to 613,700, and 20 percent kicks in above that. This only applies to investments held more than a year. Short term gains are taxed as regular income instead. Knowing these numbers can help you time a sale, especially if you're near a bracket line. Talk to a tax professional before making a big move.

topics.title: 2026 Estate Tax Exemption Jumps to $15 Million - IRS Confirms
topics.script: Here's a number that matters if you're doing estate planning. For 2026, the IRS raised the federal estate tax exemption to 15 million dollars per person. That means an individual can pass on up to 15 million dollars at death without owing any federal estate tax, and a married couple can combine their exemptions to shield 30 million dollars. This higher exemption is now permanent under the new tax law, instead of scheduled to shrink like it was before. Only estates above these amounts owe federal estate tax, so this mainly affects high net worth families. Most states also have their own separate estate or inheritance tax rules with much lower thresholds. If your estate is anywhere near these numbers, work with an estate planning attorney now.

The IRS raised the maximum adoption tax credit to 17,670 dollars per child, covering costs like adoption fees, court costs, attorney fees, and travel expenses. Here's the big change, up to 5,120 dollars of that credit is now refundable, meaning you can get that portion back as a refund even if you owe zero in taxes. That's new, this credit used to be nonrefundable for everyone. It covers domestic adoptions, foster care adoptions, and international adoptions, though the rules differ slightly by type. Keep every adoption related receipt throughout the process. File Form 8839 to claim it, and talk to a tax professional to make sure you're claiming the right amount.

topics.script: Small business owners, here's a 2026 number worth knowing before you buy equipment. The IRS raised the Section 179 deduction limit to 2,560,000 dollars for 2026. That means you can deduct the full cost of qualifying equipment, machinery, software, or business vehicles in the year you buy them, instead of depreciating it slowly over several years. The deduction starts phasing out once your total equipment purchases for the year cross 4,090,000 dollars. This is designed specifically to help small and mid sized businesses reinvest in their operations without waiting years for the tax benefit. It applies to both new and used equipment, as long as it's used more than 50 percent for business. Talk to your accountant before year end to see what qualifies.

topics.script: Here's a tax rule that mostly targets higher earners with big deductions or incentive stock options. The Alternative Minimum Tax, or AMT, runs a second set of tax rules alongside the regular system, and you pay whichever amount is higher. For 2026, the IRS raised the AMT exemption to 90,100 dollars if you're single, and 140,200 dollars if you're married filing jointly. Below those amounts, the AMT usually doesn't apply to you at all. The exemption starts phasing out once income crosses 500,000 dollars for single filers, or 1 million dollars for married couples. This mostly affects people with large state tax deductions, exercised stock options, or big itemized deductions. If any of that applies to you, run the AMT calculation before you file.

topics.script: Heads up if you're planning home upgrades this year. The IRS confirms the Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit ended for good after December 31st, 2025, and it's not available for 2026. That credit used to let homeowners claim up to 1,200 dollars a year for things like insulation, efficient windows, exterior doors, and home energy audits, plus up to 2,000 dollars for heat pumps and biomass stoves. If you installed and paid for qualifying upgrades by the end of 2025, you can still claim it on that year's tax return. But for any improvements installed in 2026 or later, this specific federal credit no longer applies. Some states and utility companies still offer their own rebates, so check those before you assume there's no help available. Always confirm current incentives before starting a project.

topics.title: 2026 Medicare Part B Premium: $202.90 - IRMAA Brackets If You Earn More
topics.script: Retiring soon or already on Medicare? Here's your 2026 number from CMS. The standard Medicare Part B premium is now 202.90 dollars a month, up from 185 dollars, and the annual deductible rose to 283 dollars. But if your income is higher, you'll pay more through something called IRMAA, the income related monthly adjustment amount. For example, if you're single and your income was above 109,000 dollars two years ago, your premium jumps to at least 284.10 dollars a month, with several higher tiers after that. IRMAA is based on your tax return from two years earlier, so your 2026 premium depends on your 2024 income. If you've had a major income drop since then, like retirement, you can file an appeal with Social Security. Check your income bracket before assuming the standard premium applies to you.
topics.description:
The standard 2026 Medicare Part B premium is $202.90 a month (deductible $283), but IRMAA surcharges push it higher for individuals earning over $109,000 or couples over $218,000, based on income from two years prior. Here's how the brackets work and how to appeal if your income has dropped.

topics.title: 2026 American Opportunity Tax Credit: Up to $2,500 Per Student (IRS)
topics.script: Paying for college this year? Make sure you're not leaving this credit on the table. The American Opportunity Tax Credit lets you claim up to 2,500 dollars per eligible student for tuition, fees, and course materials during their first four years of college. Here's the part people miss, 40 percent of that credit, up to 1,000 dollars, is refundable, meaning you can get it back even if you owe zero in taxes. For 2026, the credit phases out once your modified adjusted gross income hits 80,000 dollars if you're single, or 160,000 if you're married filing jointly, and disappears entirely at 90,000 and 180,000. You'll need Form 8863 and a 1098-T from the school to claim it. Check your income against these numbers before you file this year's return.
topics.description:
The American Opportunity Tax Credit is worth up to $2,500 per eligible student, with 40% (up to $1,000) refundable even if you owe no tax. For 2026, it phases out at $80,000-$90,000 MAGI for single filers and $160,000-$180,000 for married filing jointly.

topics.title: RMD Age Is 73 in 2026 - Miss It and Pay a 25% IRS Penalty
topics.script: If you're approaching retirement, mark this age on your calendar. Under current IRS rules, you generally must start taking required minimum distributions, or RMDs, from your traditional IRA, SIMPLE IRA, SEP IRA, or 401k once you turn 73. This age moved up thanks to the SECURE 2.0 Act, it used to be 70 and a half, then 72. The IRS calculates your RMD based on your account balance and your life expectancy factor. Here's the part that really stings, if you miss your RMD or don't take enough, the penalty is 25 percent of the amount you should have withdrawn, though it drops to 10 percent if you fix it within two years. Roth IRAs don't have this requirement during the owner's lifetime. Mark your 73rd birthday and talk to your account provider well before year end.
topics.description:
Under current IRS rules, required minimum distributions from traditional retirement accounts must generally start at age 73. Miss the deadline and the penalty is 25% of the amount you should have withdrawn (10% if corrected within two years). Here's what changed under SECURE 2.0 and how to avoid the penalty.

topics.title: Leftover 529 Funds? Roll Up to $35,000 Into a Roth IRA Tax-Free (IRS)
topics.script: Got leftover money in a 529 college savings plan? You're not stuck with it anymore. Under current IRS rules, you can roll over up to 35,000 dollars of unused 529 funds into a Roth IRA for the same beneficiary over their lifetime, completely tax and penalty free. There are a few requirements though. The 529 account has to have been open for at least 15 years, and any contributions made in the last 5 years, plus their earnings, don't qualify for the rollover. It also has to be a direct transfer from the 529 plan to the Roth IRA, and normal annual Roth contribution limits still apply each year. This is a great option if your kid got a scholarship or didn't use all the money for school. Check with your 529 plan provider on how to start the transfer.

topics.title: First-Time Homebuyers: Pull $10,000 From Your IRA Penalty-Free (IRS Rule)
topics.script: Struggling to save for a down payment? Your IRA might be able to help. Under IRS rules, first time homebuyers can withdraw up to 10,000 dollars from an IRA without paying the usual 10 percent early withdrawal penalty, even if you're under 59 and a half. This is a lifetime limit, not an annual one, and it applies per person, so a married couple could potentially pull 20,000 dollars combined. You're still considered a first time buyer if you haven't owned a home in the past two years, even if you've owned one before that. Keep in mind, this exception only waives the penalty, you'll usually still owe regular income tax on a traditional IRA withdrawal, though qualified Roth IRA withdrawals may come out tax free too. This rule only applies to IRAs, not 401k plans. Talk to a financial advisor before tapping retirement funds for a home.
topics.description:
IRS rules let first-time homebuyers withdraw up to $10,000 from an IRA without the usual 10% early withdrawal penalty, a lifetime limit per person. Here's who counts as a first-time buyer, why regular income tax may still apply, and why this only works for IRAs, not 401(k)s.

topics.title: Self-Employment Tax Explained: 15.3% You Might Not Be Budgeting For (IRS)
topics.script: If you freelance, drive for a gig app, or run your own business, this tax catches a lot of people off guard. The IRS self-employment tax rate is 15.3 percent, made up of 12.4 percent for Social Security and 2.9 percent for Medicare. As a W-2 employee, your employer normally pays half of these taxes for you, but when you're self-employed, you're responsible for both halves yourself. The good news, the IRS lets you deduct half of your self-employment tax when calculating your adjusted gross income, which softens the blow a little. This tax is separate from your regular income tax, so you owe both. Most self-employed people need to make quarterly estimated tax payments throughout the year to avoid a penalty. Use Schedule SE to calculate exactly what you owe.
topics.description:
The IRS self-employment tax rate is 15.3% (12.4% Social Security plus 2.9% Medicare), covering both the employee and employer portions that a traditional job would split. Here's why freelancers and 1099 workers owe this on top of regular income tax, and the deduction that softens it.

General education only, not personalized tax or financial advice. Source: IRS.gov (Topic no. 554, Self-Employment Tax). Consult a CPA for your specific situation.

#selfemploymenttax #freelancer #1099 #smallbusiness #IRS
